No control catches it: ctl_redemption_double_charge only compares redemptions_used to the row COUNT (both are 1 per booking, perfectly consistent); ctl_discount_charged_not_delivered compares reserved_cents to delivered (settle rewrites benefit_cents, not reserved_cents); ctl_benefit_never_settled passes because settled_at is stamped. With a loyalty tier in play it is wrong in the other direction too — a $100 gig at tierBps 800 settles the POSTER's discount campaign at promo_benefit_cents(10000,800) = 1000-800 = 200, a number derived entirely from the EARNER's tier.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql:169-194 — `for r in select * from public.promo_redemptions where booking_id = p_booking and released_at is null and settled_at is null` … `actual := least(coalesce((select max_benefit_cents ...), r.reserved_cents), public.promo_benefit_cents(p_amount_cents, r.fee_bps));` … `delta := actual - r.reserved_cents;` … `update public.promotions set spent_cents = greatest(0, spent_cents + delta) where id = r.promotion_id;` — no `join public.promotions p on p.id = r.promotion_id ... where p.kind = ...` anywhere in the loop. Compare 20260806340000_discount_kind_confusion.sql:80-87, which added exactly that scoping to the consume side. r.fee_bps for a poster discount is written at 20260806340000:126 as `coalesce(p_fee_bps, 1000)` where p_fee_bps is new.fee_bps_quoted (20260806320000:201). Call site: supabase/functions/stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:241 `supabase.rpc('settle_booking_benefits', { p_booking: bookingId, p_amount_cents: capturedGigCents })`. This is the LAST definition of settle_booking_benefits in timestamp order (only one `create or replace function public.settle_booking_benefits` exists in supabase/migrations/).
fix_sketch: Scope the settle loop by kind. Only fee_override redemptions should go through promo_benefit_cents; a poster_discount redemption's true cost IS a fixed cents amount already clamped at booking, so settle it as actual = bookings.poster_discount_cents (scaled by the capture fraction if the capture was partial), giving delta = 0 on a full capture. A bonus redemption should not be re-priced at all. Add a control asserting promotions.spent_cents >= sum of delivered poster_discount_cents for that campaign's captured bookings, since the existing three all compare counts or reserves and none compares campaign spend to money actually given away.
verifier_note: The mechanism is exactly as described. Two calibrations. (1) The loss is not unbounded - max_redemptions still binds, because settle decrements spent_cents but never redemptions_used. The real bound is max_redemptions x per-use discount, so the overshoot factor is (max_redemptions x discount)/budget_cents. At console defaults (budget $250, max_redemptions 100, $5 discount) that is 2x, not infinite; createPromotion (actions.ts:63) applies `Math.max(1, Math.round(maxRedemptions))` with no upper bound and no relation to budget, so the factor is a config choice. That residual bound is why this is high rather than critical. (2) The finding understates the observability harm: settle also writes benefit_cents = 0, so the redemption row itself records the benefit as having cost nothing, and /promotions (page.tsx:24 selects spent_cents/budget_cents) renders a burn-down that returns to ~0% after every capture - an operator watching the campaign sees a budget that is never consumed while margin is being given away. Every other consequence in the original stands.

title: ctl_discount_without_grant fires a permanent CRITICAL finding on every declined or cancelled booking that carried a poster discount
summary: release_booking_benefits deliberately does not clear bookings.poster_discount_cents (it stamps released_at on the redemption and explains why touching bookings would roll back the decline). ctl_discount_without_grant looks for exactly that state: poster_discount_cents > 0 with no redemption whose released_at is null. So the routine, intended outcome of declining an applicant permanently satisfies a critical money control's violation predicate.
trigger: Poster P holds a poster_discount grant. Earner E applies to P's gig -> pin_booking_amount stamps bookings.poster_discount_cents = 500 and inserts the redemption. P declines E (or either party cancels) -> trg_zz_release_benefits -> release_booking_benefits sets released_at, refunds the budget and returns the grant use, and leaves poster_discount_cents = 500 on the dead booking. The next hourly sweep opens a critical finding on that booking id.
money_impact: No direct money movement, but it destroys the detector built for the one bug class that DOES move money silently — a discount nobody granted (the 20260806340000 regression, where 155c came off a charge with no poster-discount campaign in existence). control_findings are unique on (control_key, entity_id) where resolved_at is null and auto-resolve only when the control stops returning the entity; a declined booking is terminal, so each of these findings is unresolvable and accumulates forever, and each new decline is a NEW critical finding — precisely the condition controls_sweep_and_page pages a human on (hourly at :05, 'emails ONLY when something newly needs a human'). Every decline by a discount-holding poster manufactures a page indistinguishable from the real thing, and once operators learn the signal is noise, the genuine ungranted-discount case is invisible.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806340000_discount_kind_confusion.sql:177-185 — `from public.bookings b where coalesce(b.poster_discount_cents, 0) > 0 and not exists (select 1 from public.promo_redemptions r join public.promotions p on p.id = r.promotion_id where r.booking_id = b.id and r.released_at is null and p.kind = 'poster_discount')`, registered at :190-199 with severity 'critical', domain 'money'. Against supabase/migrations/20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql:134 `-- DELIBERATELY DOES NOT TOUCH bookings.fee_credit_cents / poster_discount_cents.` and :127-129 `update public.promo_redemptions set released_at = now(), release_reason = p_reason where id = r.id;`, fired by trg_zz_release_benefits (:206-224) on status in ('declined','cancelled').
fix_sketch: Exclude bookings whose redemption exists but is released, and whose status is terminal: add `and b.status not in ('declined','cancelled')` plus `and not exists (... r.booking_id = b.id and p.kind='poster_discount')` without the released_at filter — i.e. the violation is 'no poster_discount redemption EVER existed for this booking', which is the actual bug shape the control was written for.
verifier_note: Confirmed, with one addition and one downgrade. ADDITION the finding missed: because run_control's upsert is `on conflict ... where resolved_at is null`, an operator who manually resolves one of these noise findings does not silence it - the next hourly sweep inserts a BRAND NEW row with created_at = now(), which lands inside the 90-minute freshness window and pages again. Closing the ticket is what makes it recur, a worse failure mode than the 'accumulates forever' described. DOWNGRADE to medium: the noise is proportional to declines by posters holding a live poster_discount grant (zero until such a campaign exists), and the control's own detail payload includes 'booking_status', so a triaging operator sees status='declined' in the alert body and can pattern-match the false positive on sight. It degrades a critical detector and manufactures pages, but moves no money and is triageable immediately - high overstates it.

title: A poster's single discount use is consumed by whichever stranger applies first, not by the hire the poster makes, and a pending application holds the campaign's budget with no control watching
summary: consume_poster_discount is called from pin_booking_amount on booking INSERT — i.e. when an EARNER applies, not when the poster accepts. The console forces uses_allowed = 1 for poster_discount, so on a multi-slot job the first applicant's booking consumes the poster's only use and every later applicant's booking is pinned at 0. If the poster hires anyone but the first applicant, the booking that actually charges carries no discount, while the campaign was charged for a booking that never billed.
trigger: Poster P holds a '$5 off your first hire' grant and posts a gig with two time slots (bookings_one_active_per_slot permits one live booking per slot, so two concurrent applications). Earner A applies to slot 1 -> discount 500 pinned to A's booking, promotions.spent_cents += 500, grant uses_consumed = 1. Earner B applies to slot 2 -> grant exhausted -> B's booking pinned at 0. P accepts B and pays full price. P then declines A, which releases the charge and returns the use — the campaign churned, the poster got nothing. Separately: if P simply ignores A rather than declining, the 500 stays charged to the campaign indefinitely.
money_impact: Two effects. (1) Non-delivery: the promise 'you get $5 off your first hire' fails for any poster who does not hire their first applicant; the campaign's redemptions_used and spent_cents both moved for a benefit worth 0 to anyone until the poster performs the extra step of declining. (2) Budget occupancy at zero attacker cost: applying is free and requires no Connect account (the hold is placed at accept time by the poster, stripe-create-payment-intent), so an account that applies to every open gig reserves one use per grant-holding poster and the campaign's full budget with no work and no money. On a $250 / $5 campaign, 50 applications exhaust the budget and every real hire during that window is priced at full rate. It self-heals only when posters decline. ctl_benefit_never_settled cannot see it: its predicate is `b.status in ('verified','declined','cancelled')` (20260806220000:314), so a reservation parked on a 'pending' booking is invisible to the control library, and the only related control, ctl_stranded_pending_booking, reports the booking without any reference to the benefit budget it is holding.

Math.max(1, Math.min(20, Math.round(uses))) : 1`. supabase/migrations/20260624220000_review5_db_fixes.sql:95-97 `create unique index ... bookings_one_active_per_slot on public.bookings (slot_id) where slot_id is not null and status in ('pending','confirmed','completed','verified')` — one live booking per SLOT, not per job, so multi-slot gigs take concurrent applications. supabase/migrations/20260806220000_benefit_lifecycle.sql:314 `and b.status in ('verified', 'declined', 'cancelled')`.
fix_sketch: Consume the poster discount at ACCEPT (when the hold is placed and the counterparty is chosen), not at application INSERT; pin it onto the booking at that moment the way fee_bps_quoted is pinned. If it must stay at INSERT, add a control for redemptions still reserved against a 'pending' booking older than N hours, and release the reservation when a competing booking on the same job is confirmed.

NARROWER: the finding's example needs concurrency, and bookings_one_active_per_slot (20260624220000:95-97, still the only definition) allows one live booking per slot - so a single-slot gig cannot exhibit this at all; the poster's only choice is accept-or-decline that one applicant, and declining self-heals via release_booking_benefits. BROADER, and this is the bigger case the finding missed: the grant is scoped to the POSTER, not the job, so the collision does not require a multi-slot gig - a poster with two open listings loses their single use to whichever applicant lands first across ANY of them, and hiring on the other listing pays full price. Separately, JobsContext.js:454 inserts `slot_id: slotId || null` and the unique index is partial on `slot_id is not null`, so null-slot bookings are not constrained to one-per-slot at all. On the budget-occupancy half: it is real but weaker than 'zero attacker cost' implies - an attacker cannot see who holds a grant, so exhausting a $250/$5 campaign means blanket-applying across the marketplace hoping to hit 50 grant-holding posters, and those same applications already grief the slot market (a consequence ctl_stranded_pending_booking's own `why` text documents), so the incremental novelty is the unwatched budget reservation rather than the DoS. Medium is right; the non-delivery half - '$5 off your first hire' silently failing - is the part worth fixing.

title: The headroom guarantee does not survive a partial capture: the platform's application fee can fall below Stripe's own processing cost when a discount consumed the headroom
summary: poster_discount_headroom guarantees fee - credit - discount >= ceil(0.029*amount) + 30 + 25 at 100% capture. The partial-capture branch scales the platform's share linearly (round(fullFee * pct)) while Stripe's fixed 30c does not scale, so for a benefit stack that consumed the headroom the application_fee_amount comes in under the real processing cost and the platform funds the difference.
trigger: A poster reports a problem and captures a fraction of a booking whose poster discount (or discount + fee credit) took most of the headroom.
money_impact: $100 gig, 1000 bps, discount 655 (full headroom), no credit: authorized amount_cents = 9345, fullFeeForAuth = platform_fee_after_credit(10000,1000,0) - 655 = 345. Poster captures 20%: captureCents = round(9345*0.2) = 1869, feeCents = min(1869, round(345*0.2)) = 69. Stripe's cost on a 1869c charge is ceil(0.029*1869) + 30 = 55 + 30 = 85. The platform collects 69 and pays 85 — 16c out of pocket, the exact outcome the floor exists to prevent. Deficit is bounded: it is 55*pct + 0.029*pct*D - 30, so it is negative for pct below ~0.55 and never worse than ~30c per booking. Small, but it is a real breach of the stated invariant ('a credit reduces OUR margin, never Stripe's costs') and it scales with the number of disputed captures.
evidence: supabase/functions/stripe-capture-payment/index.ts:144-179 — `const discountCents = Math.max(0, Math.trunc(Number(payment.poster_discount_cents) || 0));` … `const fullFeeForAuth = Math.max(0, Number(fullFeeCalc) - discountCents);` … `const captureCents = Math.max(1, Math.round((payment.amount_cents || 0) * capturePct));` … `const feeCents = Math.min(captureCents, Math.round(fullFeeCents * capturePct));` — the fee is scaled by pct with no re-application of the processing floor. The floor itself: supabase/migrations/20260806080000_referral_bonus.sql:46-58 `platform_fee_after_credit` = greatest(ceil(amount*0.029)+30+25, fee - credit).
fix_sketch: Re-floor the scaled fee against the CAPTURED amount rather than scaling the authorized-amount fee: feeCents = max(min(captureCents, round(fullFee*pct)), ceil(0.029*captureCents) + 30) — i.e. call platform_fee_after_credit again on the captured figure and subtract a proportionally scaled discount, so the fixed 30c is charged once in full at whatever amount actually settles.
verifier_note: Directionally right, mechanically and economically wrong in three ways. (1) capturePct is hard-floored at 0.5 (index.ts:70), so the 20%-capture example - and with it the 16c figure and the 'negative for pct below ~0.55' analysis - cannot happen. Over the legal range [0.5, 1] the maximum out-of-pocket is 2-3 cents per booking, not 16-30. (2) The poster discount is NOT the cause, and the finding's own discount example is safely positive (+7c). What drives the fee to the floor is anything that makes platform_fee_after_credit bind: a FULL FEE CREDIT ($100 gig, credit 655, no discount -> capture 5000, fee 173, Stripe cost 175, margin -2c), or simply a small gig whose base fee already sits at the floor - the grid's worst case was a $5 gig at 500 bps with NO discount and NO credit (capture 250, fee 35, cost 38, margin -3c). The correct statement is 'any 50% partial capture of a booking whose full fee is at or near the processing floor', and rewriting only the discount path would not fix it. (3) The fix sketch is right in shape - re-floor against the CAPTURED amount, feeCents = max(min(captureCents, round(fullFee*pct)), ceil(0.029*captureCents) + 30) - but it must apply unconditionally, not only when a discount is present. Severity stays low: at 2-3 cents per disputed partial capture this is a correctness blemish on a stated invariant, not a money problem.

title: Promo cost is measured against the standing rate, blind to the loyalty tier — the campaign is charged (and a grant use burned) for a benefit the tier already delivered, or for nothing at all
summary: pin_booking_amount applies the tier first (fee_bps_quoted := least(standing, tierBps)) and then calls consume_promo_grant WITHOUT passing the already-lowered rate. consume_promo_grant charges the campaign promo_benefit_cents(amount, grant_bps) = fee@fee_bps_at(now()) − fee@grant_bps — i.e. it counterfactuals against the STANDING rate, not against the tier rate the earner would actually otherwise have paid. Whenever the earner's tier rate is at or below the grant's rate, the promo changes the pin by zero or by less than it was charged, but promotions.spent_cents and redemptions_used are incremented, promo_grants.uses_consumed is burned, and a promo_redemptions row is written. settle_booking_benefits at capture recomputes with the same tier-blind promo_benefit_cents (line 176-179), so the overcharge is never corrected — it is baked in permanently.
trigger: Any enabled fee_tier rung + any active kind='fee_override' promotion. Concretely: standing rate 1000 bps; earner stands on the seeded 'Veteran' rung (700 bps, 20260806120000_fee_tiers.sql:216); a live campaign grants 800 bps. Earner books a $100 gig. Pin: fee_bps_quoted = least(1000, 700) = 700. consume_promo_grant finds the 800-bps grant, charges hit = least(max_benefit_cents, promo_benefit_cents(10000, 800)) = 1000c − 800c = 200c, increments redemptions_used, burns a use, inserts a redemption. Returns 800. Pin then does least(700, 800) = 700 — the promo moved nothing.
money_impact: Case A (promo bps >= tier bps): campaign charged 200c, delivered 0c, user's grant use destroyed. A 50,000c budget is exhausted after 250 such bookings having delivered zero discount to anyone; the campaign then stops working for earners who are NOT on a tier and would have benefited. Case B (promo bps < tier bps, e.g. promo 500 vs tier 700 on $100): real delivered benefit = fee 700c → 500c = 200c, but the campaign is charged 1000c − 500c = 500c. Overcharge = 300c per booking, exactly the tier's own contribution. Budget therefore bounds 60% less real discount than intended, and every 'how much did this campaign cost us' number in /promotions is inflated by the tier's share of the discount. promo_redemptions.fee_bps also records 800 (the grant) rather than 700 (what was actually pinned), so the audit trail disagrees with the charge.
fix_sketch: Pass the already-pinned rate into the promo path and counterfactual against it: consume_promo_grant(p_user, p_booking, p_amount_cents, p_baseline_bps) with hit := least(max_benefit_cents, platform_fee_cents(amount, p_baseline_bps) - platform_fee_cents(amount, g.fee_bps)), and return null (charging nothing, burning nothing) when g.fee_bps >= p_baseline_bps. Do the same in settle_booking_benefits by storing the baseline on promo_redemptions. Add a control mirroring ctl_discount_charged_not_delivered for kind='fee_override': flag redemptions where reserved_cents > 0 and bookings.fee_bps_quoted >= r.fee_bps.
verifier_note: Severity downgraded critical → high. Two of the finding's framings overstate the harm. (1) No user is overcharged and no money leaves the platform incorrectly: lowest-wins means the earner is always pinned at the best available rate, so the direction of the defect is that the platform KEEPS more than the campaign is billed for. The losses are (a) campaign budget consumed for undelivered benefit, so a budget bounds up to 60% less real discount than intended and exhausts early on non-tiered earners who would have benefited, (b) the earner's grant use is destroyed for nothing, and (c) every campaign-cost number on /promotions is inflated by the tier's share. That is squarely finding class #2 (charged but not delivered) but not class #1 (unbounded loss) — promotions.budget_cents and max_redemptions still bound the spend, they just bound the wrong quantity. (2) The bug is currently DORMANT: 20260806120000_fee_tiers.sql:214-218 seeds all three rungs with enabled=false ('Seed a sensible ladder, DISABLED'), and tier_fee_bps filters `where t.enabled`, so it returns NULL and the tier least() is a no-op today. It becomes live the moment an admin clicks setTier — one click, which is the whole point of the feature — after which it fires deterministically on every booking by a tiered earner holding a fee_override grant. The proposed fix (pass the pinned baseline into consume_promo_grant, return null without charging when g.fee_bps >= baseline, store the baseline on promo_redemptions for settle, and widen ctl_discount_charged_not_delivered to kind='fee_override') is correct.

title: The tier threshold is a bare count of verified bookings with no amount weighting and no counterparty diversity — a permanent 300 bps discount is farmable for about $44.50 through a second account
summary: earner_completed_count counts every booking with status='verified' regardless of gross value, counterparty, or whether the two accounts are the same person. The migration's own header asserts this is uninflatable ('It counts VERIFIED bookings — work that was actually completed and paid for. Anything a user can inflate on their own ... would be a tier you could self-assign'), and the only barrier is that guard_bookings_write requires a captured payment before a booking can reach 'verified'. That makes each count-increment cost exactly one platform fee on a minimum-priced gig, not one unit of real work. Nothing checks that the 50 counterparties are 50 different people, and no ctl_* control watches booking concentration between a poster/earner pair. Tiers have no budget, no expiry and no re-evaluation, so the yield is unbounded and permanent.
trigger: Attacker holds two accounts, A (poster, saved card) and B (earner, Stripe Connect onboarded). A posts a $10 gig (the floor, guard_job_pay_floor). B applies; guard only blocks earner_id = poster_id, which two distinct accounts do not trip. A accepts (hold placed), both mark done, A verifies -> capture -> status 'verified'. Repeat. No work is performed and no third party is involved.
money_impact: Cost per increment is the platform fee on a $10 gig, and it FALLS as the farmer climbs: platform_fee_cents(1000, 1000)=100c; at the 900-bps rung max(90, floor 84)=90c; at the 800-bps rung max(80,84)=84c. Reaching 'Veteran' (50 verified, 700 bps) therefore costs 10x100 + 15x90 + 25x84 = 4450c = $44.50 out of pocket (the poster account's $10 returns to the earner account minus the fee). Yield: 300 bps off every future gig, forever, with no expiry and no budget. On $100 gigs that is $3.00/gig -> break-even at 15 real gigs; an earner doing $2,000/month of GMV keeps $60/month indefinitely. The platform's exposure is unbounded because, unlike a promotion, a tier has no budget_cents and no max_redemptions to stop it. Note also that the farming traffic itself passes AML/fraud-free through Stripe as ~50 round-trip card charges between two accounts controlled by one person.
evidence:
supabase/migrations/20260806120000_fee_tiers.sql:58-68 — the entire eligibility test:
  select coalesce(count(*), 0)::int
    from public.bookings b
   where b.earner_id = p_user and b.status = 'verified'

supabase/migrations/20260806120000_fee_tiers.sql:19-20 (the claim this defeats):
-- THE THRESHOLD IS DERIVED, NOT DECLARED. It counts VERIFIED bookings — work that was
-- actually completed and paid for. Anything a user can inflate on their own ... would be a tier you could self-assign.

The only anti-self-deal check, supabase/migrations/20260730140000_pin_booking_insert_columns.sql:87:
    if new.earner_id = poster then
      raise exception 'You cannot book your own gig';

The pay floor that sets the unit cost, supabase/migrations/20260728120000_min_job_pay_floor.sql:41-42:
    if new.pay is null or new.pay < 10 then
      raise exception 'Gigs must pay at least $10 (got %)', new.pay

Control registry contains fee_tier_below_floor and fee_tier_ladder_inverted only — no control covers tier eligibility integrity or booking concentration between a pair (grep of all `('<key>',` rows in supabase/migrations/).
fix_sketch: Make the threshold resistant to cheap repetition: count DISTINCT posters (or require min_distinct_posters alongside min_completed), and/or gate on cumulative verified GMV rather than a raw count so a $10 booking contributes $10 of progress rather than a whole rung. Add a ctl_* control that flags any earner whose verified bookings are concentrated on one or two poster_ids above a threshold, and re-run tier eligibility exclusions for refunded/disputed bookings.
verifier_note: Severity downgraded high → medium, and the economics in money_impact are wrong in the platform's favour. The yield is NOT '300 bps off every future gig, forever' as marginal extra: the tier is legitimately attainable by any earner who does 50 real gigs, so what $44.50 buys is ACCELERATION, and the platform's loss is bounded by the ladder differential over the first 50 real gigs, not unbounded. On $100 gigs that differential is 10×$3 + 15×$2 + 25×$1 = $85, against $44.50 of cost — net +$40.50 to the farmer, a ~1.9x return. The attack is genuinely profitable, and sharply more so for high-ticket earners: on $500 gigs the differential is 10×$15 + 15×$10 + 25×$5 = $425 for the same $44.50 (~9.5x), and on $2,000 gigs ~$1,700 (~38x). So 'profitable' is proven; 'unbounded' and '$60/month indefinitely' are not. Two further corrections: the platform does not even collect the $44.50 — at the 800/700 rungs the fee is pinned at the processing floor, so of the farmer's 4450c the platform nets only 10×16 + 15×6 + 25×0 = 250c ($2.50) and Stripe takes ~$42; and the whole exploit is dormant today because all three rungs are seeded enabled=false (20260806120000:214-218), so it costs nothing until an admin enables a rung. The fix sketch (distinct-poster requirement or cumulative verified GMV instead of a raw count, plus a concentration control and exclusion of refunded/disputed bookings) is the right shape.

title: No client surface reads fee_tiers or tier_fee_bps — the margin is spent and the retention it was bought for is never delivered, and the pre-booking quote misstates the earner's net
summary: Zero code in src/, web/, shared/ or supabase/functions/ references fee_tiers, tier_fee_bps or earner_completed_count — the only consumers in the entire repo are the admin console's /pricing page. The migration explicitly granted SELECT on fee_tiers to authenticated precisely so users could see the ladder ('someone should be able to see the ladder they are climbing, and "do 10 more gigs and your fee drops" is the entire retention mechanic'), and that grant is unused. Separately, the earner's quote screen computes 'You receive' and 'GoHustlr is taking X%' from getFeeBps() (the standing rate only), so a tiered earner is quoted a fee strictly higher than the one the pin will stamp — and then sees a different, unexplained rate on the booking afterwards, because every post-booking surface correctly uses booking.fee_bps_quoted.
trigger: An admin enables any rung via /pricing (setTier). Every earner past that threshold is immediately pinned at the lower rate on every new booking, and is never told — not on the ladder, not on the quote, not on the confirmation. The only way to notice is to compare the pre-booking 'You receive' against the post-booking figure.
money_impact: At the seeded 'Veteran' rung the platform gives up 300 bps of every gig by its highest-volume earners, permanently and with no budget ceiling — $3.00 on every $100 gig — in exchange for a retention effect that cannot occur, because no earner is ever informed the ladder exists or that they are on it. The disclosure direction is in the user's favour (quoted 10%, charged 7%), so it is not a consumer-harm overcharge, but it means the sole justification for the spend (a credible 'stay and your rate drops' signal against off-platform leakage) is not being delivered.
fix_sketch: Add a tier-aware quote: an RPC (or a my_profile() field) returning tier_fee_bps(auth.uid()) plus the next rung and the gap to it, and have JobDetailScreen/web quote screens use least(standing, tier) for the 'You receive' figure. Surface the ladder itself on the Profile/Money screen from the already-granted fee_tiers SELECT.
verifier_note: Severity downgraded medium → low, on three grounds. (1) Zero impact today: all three rungs are seeded enabled=false (20260806120000:214-218) and tier_fee_bps filters on t.enabled, so no earner is currently tiered and the quote is accurate for everyone. (2) The disclosure error runs in the user's favour — quoted 10%, charged 7% — so it is not a consumer-harm overcharge and is not the class of disclosure bug src/lib/pricing.js's own header warns about (that one is about showing today's rate on an already-pinned booking, which the code does correctly). (3) The 'retention is never delivered' half is a product-strategy argument about whether a margin decision achieves its purpose, not a broken invariant; it is not a money-loss, authorization, kill-switch or control finding. What remains genuinely worth fixing is narrow and concrete: if a rung is ever enabled, the pre-booking quote will understate the earner's net, and the fee_tiers SELECT grant that was created specifically to make the ladder visible has no consumer. The fix sketch is correct.

title: A failed tier lookup is downgraded to a Postgres log warning and nothing verifies that a booking's pinned rate honoured the tier — the earner is silently charged full fee and no control can tell
summary: The tier block in pin_booking_amount is wrapped in `exception when others then raise warning`, so any failure (statement timeout on the unindexed count over bookings, a permission or search_path regression on tier_fee_bps, a future refactor that renames the function) results in fee_bps_quoted silently staying at the standing rate. The warning lands in the Postgres log, not in control_findings, not in client_errors, and not in any alert dispatch path. The two tier controls that exist check only CONFIGURATION (ctl_fee_tier_below_floor, ctl_fee_tier_ladder_inverted); no control checks DELIVERY — i.e. that bookings.fee_bps_quoted <= tier_fee_bps(earner_id) for bookings created while a rung was enabled. The equivalent delivery control was built for the poster discount and scoped to that kind only. There is also no jest coverage of tiers (no __tests__ file references them), so the drift guard that protects category_slug and platform_fee_cents does not exist here.
trigger: tier_fee_bps raises for any reason during a booking INSERT — e.g. bookings grows and the unindexed `count(*) ... where earner_id = ? and status='verified'` (no index on bookings(earner_id) exists anywhere in supabase/schema.sql or supabase/migrations/) exceeds statement_timeout under load. Every booking inserted during that window pins the standing rate. Nothing pages, nothing opens a finding, and because no client shows the tier the earner has no way to notice either.
money_impact: Each affected booking overcharges the earner by the tier delta — 300 bps at the Veteran rung, $3.00 on a $100 gig — pinned immutably (pin_booking_amount rewrites fee_bps_quoted back to old on any non-service_role UPDATE), so it cannot be corrected after the fact without a service-role write. Because the failure is silent on both the operator side and the user side, the outage is unbounded in duration: this is the same shape as the alert-dispatch GUC that sat dead from 2026-07-10 to 2026-08-06.
fix_sketch: Add ctl_tier_not_honoured: for bookings created since the earliest enabled rung, flag any row where fee_bps_quoted > tier_fee_bps(earner_id) computed as of created_at. Record the swallowed exception into control_findings (or client_errors) rather than only raise warning. Add `create index on public.bookings (earner_id, status)` so the eligibility count cannot be the thing that times out.
verifier_note: Severity downgraded medium → low, because the stated trigger does not hold up and the residual is thinner than claimed. The concrete failure path offered — statement_timeout on the unindexed count — is not credible: the count runs inside a SECURITY DEFINER trigger over a pre-launch bookings table of at most thousands of rows, against Supabase's multi-second statement_timeout; it would take millions of rows to bite, at which point the missing index would be causing visible pain everywhere else first. The other suggested causes (permission or search_path regression) are foreclosed by the function being SECURITY DEFINER with `set search_path = public`. So the practical trigger is a future refactor, not a live fault. Two further corrections: the exception handler is not an oversight but the consistent house pattern — the identical `exception when others` wrapper guards the promo, fee-credit and poster-discount blocks in the same function, and failing open to the standing rate keeps the booking succeeding rather than blocking it, which is the defensible direction for a benefit lookup. And the whole path is dormant while all rungs are seeded enabled=false. What genuinely survives is the class-7 point alone: no control asserts that a pinned rate honoured an enabled tier, so a delivery failure would be invisible on both the operator and user side (the latter reinforced by no client surfacing the tier). Note that such a control needs as-of-created_at logic — a booking pinned before a rung was enabled, or before the earner crossed the threshold, legitimately has fee_bps_quoted > today's tier_fee_bps, so the naive query in the fix sketch would be all false positives.

title: saveTier can re-rate or re-threshold a LIVE rung with no confirmation, while deleteTier refuses to touch a live rung — the same harm, guarded on one path only
summary: deleteTier explicitly refuses to remove an enabled rung on the grounds that 'deleting a live rung silently raises the fee for everyone on it'. saveTier performs an unconditional UPDATE of name, min_completed and fee_bps on any tier including an enabled one, with no typed confirmation and no enabled check — and raising fee_bps from 700 to 900, or raising min_completed from 50 to 500, produces exactly the harm deleteTier is written to prevent. setPlatformRate, the analogous write, demands a typed 'CHANGE RATE' plus a mandatory note; saveTier requires neither. Both are admin-tier + requireFreshAdmin(300s) + audited, so this is a consistency/blast-radius gap rather than an authorization gap.
trigger: An admin edits a live rung's fee percentage or threshold in the inline TierEditor (admin/app/(console)/pricing/PricingControls.tsx:129-176 — every field is editable in place, one Save click, no confirm step).
money_impact: Direction of harm is toward the earner: every earner standing on that rung is silently moved to a higher fee on all future bookings, with no notice, no note recorded explaining why, and — because no client surface shows the tier at all (see the invisibility finding) — no possibility of the affected earners noticing. At the seeded rungs that is up to 300 bps, $3.00 per $100 gig, across the platform's highest-volume earners. Already-pinned bookings are correctly unaffected.
fix_sketch: In saveTier, when the target row is enabled AND fee_bps is increasing or min_completed is increasing, require the same typed confirmation and mandatory note that setPlatformRate demands, and include the before/after values in the audit payload (today the audit records only the new `row`, so the previous rate is not recoverable from the log).
verifier_note: Two refinements that slightly reframe it. First, deleteTier's guard is a speed bump rather than a real gate — an admin can call setTier to disable and then deleteTier, two clicks, so the asymmetry is between 'two clicks' and 'one click', not between 'blocked' and 'allowed'. That makes the finding a UX-consistency gap rather than a missing control, which is why low is the right severity. Second, saveTier's header comment at :138-142 already reasons explicitly about edit safety ('every booking PINS its rate at INSERT, so a change reaches future bookings only and can never re-price work already agreed') — that reasoning is correct and I confirmed it against the last-writer pin, whose UPDATE branch (20260806320000:207-214) rewrites fee_bps_quoted back to old for any non-service_role caller. So already-agreed work is genuinely protected; the gap is confined to future bookings by earners standing on the edited rung, compounded by the fact that no client surface shows them the tier (see finding 3), so they cannot notice. Impact is bounded at 300 bps on the seeded ladder and is currently zero because no rung is enabled.

title: Turning off the alert-dispatch flags kills all alerting permanently and no control can see it — the 2026-07-10 silent death, recurring with a different key
summary: app_flags.controls_alert.enabled=false (or safety_alert.enabled=false, or a blanked value.url) makes every dispatcher early-return BEFORE net.http_post. The only control watching alerting, ctl_alert_dispatch_failing, reads net._http_response — i.e. it can only observe dispatches that were ATTEMPTED and came back non-2xx. A dispatch that is never attempted produces no row, so the control returns zero rows, its finding auto-resolves, and /controls renders green. The migration that moved this config out of a GUC explicitly promised the opposite.
trigger: An admin (admin tier + fresh MFA) flips controls_alert or safety_alert to off on /flags — legitimately, e.g. to stop paging during a noisy incident — and never flips it back. Or someone edits app_flags.value and blanks 'url'. From that moment: controls_sweep_and_page returns at `if not on_ then return` (20260806330000:69), controls_digest returns at `if not on_ or url is null then return` (20260806030000:86), notify_safety_report returns at `if not on_ or url is null then return` (20260806020000:85). Controls still run and still write findings, so nothing errors and nothing goes stale; ctl_control_disabled (20260806280000:38) only inspects public.controls rows, not app_flags; ctl_alert_dispatch_failing sees an empty net._http_response window. No email ever arrives again, including the daily digest that would otherwise be the reminder.
money_impact: Detection loss, not a direct debit. Every money control in the framework (money_exposed_on_dead_booking, settled_without_captured_payment, payment_ledger_impossible, discount_charged_not_delivered, redemption_double_charge, benefit_never_settled, stripe_reconciliation) keeps writing findings that nobody is told about, so any loss those controls bound becomes unbounded in TIME — it accrues until a human happens to open /controls. Safety side: with safety_alert off, every harassment/assault report saves silently and pages nobody, which is exactly the state that existed 2026-07-10 → 2026-08-06 and that 20260806020000 was written to end. Note the asymmetry the codebase itself established for controls: a disabled CONTROL auto-re-enables after 24h (trg_z_control_disable_expires + reenable_expired_controls, 20260806350000) and costs a daily finding; a disabled FLAG has no expiry and costs nothing.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806160000_dispatch_monitoring.sql:34-36 — `from net._http_response r where r.created > now() - interval '25 hours' and (r.status_code is null or r.status_code < 200 or r.status_code >= 300)`. It can only see attempts. Compare the promise in supabase/migrations/20260806020000_alert_config_in_app_flags.sql:27 — "a control can now check 'is alerting configured?' and page if not" — and 20260806030000_schedule_controls.sql:22-24 — "the config can be READ BACK and asserted on by a control. That is what makes 'is our alerting actually wired up?' a checkable question". No such control exists: the full registry (39 keys) contains alert_dispatch_failing and control_disabled and nothing that reads app_flags. The early returns: 20260806330000_dispatch_timeouts.sql:45,69 `on_ := coalesce((select enabled from public.app_flags where key = 'controls_alert'), true); … if not on_ then return; end if;`; 20260806030000_schedule_controls.sql:82,86; 20260806020000_alert_config_in_app_flags.sql:81,85.
fix_sketch: Add ctl_alert_not_dispatching: a control that reads app_flags directly and returns a row for each of ('safety_alert','controls_alert') where the key is MISSING, enabled=false, value->>'url' is null/empty, or value->>'secret' is null/empty — plus a row when max(net._http_response.created) for the controls-alert URL is older than ~2 hours (proof of liveness, not just absence of failure). Cover the missing-key case explicitly: `select 'safety_alert' where not exists (select 1 from app_flags where key='safety_alert')`. Then give app_flags the same auto-expiry the controls table got: a disabled_until column + a trigger that re-enables an off flag after 24h, so silencing alerting is a decision that must be renewed rather than forgotten. A finding from this control still cannot be emailed while dispatch is off, so also surface it as a persistent red banner on /controls and /flags.
verifier_note: Two refinements the finding gets wrong or omits, plus a severity downgrade. (1) The state is NOT invisible: admin/app/(console)/flags/page.tsx:46-52 renders a permanent red banner listing every paused flag by key, so controls_alert=off IS displayed — it is unmonitored and absent from /controls, not undisplayed. (2) The two off-switch shapes are not equivalent. With enabled=false the final sweep body still dispatches reconcile-stripe (the `if not on_ then return` sits AFTER the reconcile block, 20260806330000:69), so net._http_response keeps receiving rows and the external stripe_reconciliation control stays fresh — blindness is total, as claimed. But blanking value.url returns at `if url is null` BEFORE the reconcile dispatch, which additionally stops Stripe reconciliation entirely and makes that control go stale past 6h, which /controls page.tsx:50-53 does render — so the url-blanking variant leaves one visible tell that enabled=false does not. The proposed liveness probe must therefore key on the controls-alert URL specifically, since reconcile rows keep arriving either way. (3) Critical is overstated: no money moves as a direct consequence, the act requires admin tier plus fresh MFA, and it writes an audit row (flag.disable). This is the same class of detection-truthfulness defect the codebase itself rates 'high' for control_disabled and alert_dispatch_failing.

title: ctl_stripe_id_mode_mismatch is gated on an app_flags key that no migration ever creates and the console cannot create — it is structurally incapable of firing
summary: The control's every branch is predicated on `mode.m = 'live'`, where m comes from `app_flags.stripe_mode.value->>'mode'` defaulted to 'test'. Grep of the entire repo finds exactly two references to 'stripe_mode' — both are this read. No migration seeds the row, and the console's setFlag refuses unknown keys and only ever writes `enabled`, never `value`. So the control returns zero rows unconditionally, records last_violations=0 / last_error=null, and reports itself healthy forever.
trigger: The live Stripe cutover. The control was registered specifically because "there are 7 connected accounts and 4 customers holding test ids right now" and this is "the single most likely way the live cutover breaks" (20260806350000:30-33). On cutover day the operator flips Stripe to live keys, opens /controls, sees stripe_id_mode_mismatch green with 0 violations, and concludes the stored ids are clean. They are not — the check never ran a comparison, because nobody inserted an app_flags row that no migration creates and no console page can create.
money_impact: Every poster who tries to pay an earner holding a test-mode acct_ id gets a hard Stripe failure at the moment of payment — the booking cannot be funded, so it cannot be confirmed (accept-booking requires a real authorized PaymentIntent), and the earner cannot be paid for work already agreed. The control exists to catch this BEFORE cutover; blind, it converts a pre-flight check into a live outage across the 7 accounts and 4 customers the migration itself counted.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806350000_controls_always_on.sql:180-201 — `with mode as (select coalesce((select value->>'mode' from public.app_flags where key = 'stripe_mode'), 'test') m) … where mode.m = 'live' and a.account_id like 'acct_1%' … where mode.m = 'live' and c.customer_id like 'cus_%'`. Repo-wide: `grep -rn "stripe_mode" . --exclude-dir=node_modules` returns only 20260806350000:173 (a comment) and :182 (this read) — no INSERT anywhere. admin/app/(console)/flags/actions.ts:42-50 updates only `{enabled, updated_by, updated_at}` and hard-fails on an unseeded key: "No flag named … Flags are seeded by migration, not created here."
fix_sketch: Seed the row in a migration — `insert into app_flags (key, enabled, value, note) values ('stripe_mode', true, jsonb_build_object('mode','test'), '…') on conflict do nothing` — and make the control fail LOUD rather than silent when the declared mode is absent: return a finding of its own ('stripe mode is not declared, so id-mode checking is off') instead of defaulting to 'test'. A control whose predicate is unsatisfiable must report that fact, not zero.
verifier_note: The finding understates the defect and overstates the money impact. Understates: even if someone hand-inserted stripe_mode with mode='live' in the SQL editor, the predicate cannot do the job it claims. Stripe acct_/cus_ ids are not structurally distinguishable by mode — this repo's own sandbox (test-mode) account, RUNBOOK_MONEY.md:188 `acct_1ThvnME0UZFlVCOp`, is 21 characters, so `account_id like 'acct_1%' and length(account_id) < 22` matches it, and a live acct_ id has the identical 21-character shape and matches too; same for `cus_%` with `length < 19` (cus_ ids are 18). Armed, the control flags 100% of stored ids regardless of mode; unarmed it flags none. It is useless in both directions, not a working check that is merely unswitched — so the fix is not just seeding the row, it is replacing the heuristic (the migration's own comment at :169-172 concedes the only reliable signal is that a live key cannot retrieve a test id, i.e. an API round-trip that belongs in the external reconcile-stripe control). Overstates: 'converts a pre-flight check into a live outage' assumes working coverage was lost. None ever existed. This stands as a category-7 finding (a control reporting success while blind) at high, not as a money-loss finding.

title: The daily controls digest still dispatches at pg_net's 5s default while its handler makes a synchronous Anthropic call — a guaranteed daily false HIGH on the one channel that must never cry wolf
summary: 20260806330000 raised net.http_post timeouts to 120s (reconcile) and 30s (page) precisely because a 5s timeout wrote a null-status row that ctl_alert_dispatch_failing reported as the alerting channel being broken. It redefined only controls_sweep_and_page. controls_digest was never redefined — it is still the 20260806030000 body with no timeout_milliseconds, i.e. 5000ms — and the digest is the mode that calls api.anthropic.com synchronously (claude-sonnet-5, max_tokens 1200) before sending the Resend email.
trigger: 13:05 UTC daily. cron job controls_digest → controls_digest() → net.http_post(url, body {mode:'digest'}) with the 5s default. controls-alert:131 enters the triage branch whenever ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set (DEPLOYMENT.md:107 lists it as configured ✅) and there is at least one open finding, errored control, or stale control, and awaits a 1200-token completion plus a Resend POST. That does not return in 5s. pg_net abandons the wait and writes a net._http_response row with status_code null. At the 14:05 sweep, ctl_alert_dispatch_failing returns that row's id as a NEW entity_id, a fresh HIGH finding opens, and controls-alert pages: "an alert or reconciliation dispatch did not return 2xx — the channel that tells you about problems is itself failing." The finding persists 25h, then repeats with a new id the next day.
money_impact: No direct debit; it destroys the credibility of the money-alerting channel. The migration that fixed the identical mechanism for the sweep records the cost in its own words: "Three findings had accumulated from this, at high severity, on the one channel that must never cry wolf. Alert fatigue is the failure mode the whole control framework exists to avoid." A daily false HIGH claiming detection is down trains the on-call to dismiss exactly the alert that would announce a real dispatch failure — after which a genuine 404/403 from a rotated controls_alert secret is indistinguishable from the daily noise, and every money control's output stops being delivered without anyone noticing.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806030000_schedule_controls.sql:89-94 — `perform net.http_post(url := url, headers := …, body := jsonb_build_object('mode','digest'));` with no timeout argument; this is the only definition of controls_digest (grep: 20260806330000 redefines controls_sweep_and_page only). supabase/functions/controls-alert/index.ts:130-166 — `const anthropicKey = Deno.env.get('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'); if (mode === 'digest' && anthropicKey && (…)) { … await fetch('https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages', { … max_tokens: 1200 … }) }`, awaited inline before the Resend send at :204. supabase/migrations/20260806330000_dispatch_timeouts.sql:9-14 documents the exact failure mode for the sweep: "pg_net abandoned the wait, wrote a row with status_code null and 'Timeout of 5000 ms reached', and ctl_alert_dispatch_failing correctly reported that a dispatch did not return 2xx." DEPLOYMENT.md:107 confirms ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set.
fix_sketch: Redefine controls_digest with `timeout_milliseconds := 120000` (the digest does more work than the page it was compared to). Independently, make ctl_alert_dispatch_failing distinguish a client-side timeout (status_code null + 'Timeout' in error_msg) from a real non-2xx response and rank the former lower, so a slow-but-successful handler can never be reported as a broken channel.
verifier_note: Three mechanical corrections and a severity downgrade. (1) Not unconditional: index.ts:131 gates triage on `mode === 'digest' && anthropicKey && (open.length || errored.length || stale.length)`, so a genuinely clean board yields a fast digest and no timeout row. It is however SELF-SUSTAINING once it fires even once, because the timeout row itself becomes an open finding, guaranteeing open.length >= 1 the next morning — a stronger argument than 'guaranteed' and the one the finding should make. (2) The digest EMAIL still arrives: pg_net abandoning the wait does not kill the edge function, which 20260806330000:13-14 records verbatim for reconcile-stripe ('The request had been made, the function ran to completion'). No information is lost; the damage is a spurious HIGH finding plus one page. (3) Duration is likely shorter than the claimed 25h — pg_net's worker deletes net._http_response rows on a TTL (~6h by default), so the finding probably opens at the 14:05 sweep and auto-resolves the same evening: one false page per morning rather than a permanently open finding. Settling that needs a runtime `select min(created), max(created) from net._http_response`, which I am forbidden to run; it does not change the direction. Severity: no money moves and no detection is actually lost, only credibility — medium, not high.

title: promotions_enabled does not switch off referral fee credits or loyalty tiers, while the console asserts "All promotions are switched off"
summary: The flag is checked in redeem_promo_code, consume_promo_grant and consume_poster_discount. It is checked in NONE of the other three incentive paths the pin runs: tier_fee_bps (loyalty), accrue_referral_bonus (creates bonus_ledger rows and charges a bonus campaign's budget), and consume_fee_credit (spends those credits against the platform fee on every new booking). So the documented "everything off at once. Incident switch." leaves half the incentive surface live, and the /promotions page tells the operator the opposite in bold.
trigger: An incentive-abuse incident. An admin flips promotions_enabled OFF on /flags and reads the /promotions banner: "All promotions are switched off … No code redeems and no grant applies to a new booking." Referral credits keep flowing regardless: every booking INSERT still runs pin_booking_amount → tier_fee_bps (line 121 of the live pin) and → consume_fee_credit (line 187), neither of which consults any flag; every booking that reaches 'verified' still fires trg_z_accrue_referral_bonus, which charges the active kind='bonus' campaign's budget_cents and mints a new pending credit. The only remaining lever is hand-written SQL against promotions.status or fee_tiers.enabled.
money_impact: Per booking, a credit-holding earner takes the whole gap between the platform fee and the Stripe processing floor. $100 gig at the standing 1000 bps: fee 1000c, floor = ceil(10000*0.029)+30+25 = 345c, headroom 655c — so up to $6.55 of platform margin per booking continues to be given away with the master switch reading OFF, and it keeps going until the ledger is drained. Unlike promotions, bonus_ledger has no budget_cents of its own: its ceiling is whatever the bonus campaign already accrued, and accrual itself continues while the switch is off. Loyalty tiers (a standing rate cut with, per the pin's own comment, "no budget, no expiry") have no kill switch at all — not this one, not any.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806080000_referral_bonus.sql:160-206 consume_fee_credit — no app_flags read anywhere in the body; :60-113 accrue_referral_bonus — same; :125-155 vest_bonuses — same. supabase/migrations/20260806120000_fee_tiers.sql:74-88 tier_fee_bps — same. The live pin (supabase/migrations/20260806320000_discount_headroom_after_credit.sql:141-215) calls all four: `tierBps := public.tier_fee_bps(new.earner_id)` (:121 of that body), `consume_promo_grant` (flag-gated), `consume_fee_credit` (:187, ungated), `consume_poster_discount` (flag-gated). The claim: supabase/migrations/20260806070000_promotions.sql:24 "app_flags.promotions_enabled = false → everything off at once. Incident switch." and :215-218 "Master switch for ALL promotions." The console assertion: admin/app/(console)/promotions/page.tsx:50-56 renders "All promotions are switched off … No code redeems and no grant applies to a new booking" directly above the live Bonus payable / pending / applied tiles.
fix_sketch: Either (a) add the same `if not coalesce((select enabled from app_flags where key='promotions_enabled'), true) then return 0; end if;` guard to consume_fee_credit and accrue_referral_bonus and have tier_fee_bps consult a new 'fee_tiers_enabled' flag — noting that gating consume_fee_credit is the right direction (the credit stays on the ledger, unspent, and release_booking_benefits already returns credits, so nothing is forfeited); or (b) keep them ungated deliberately and fix the two texts: seed the note as "promo codes, fee-override grants and poster discounts only — referral credits and loyalty tiers are NOT covered", and change the /promotions banner to name what is and is not off. Whichever is chosen, the flag's stated scope and its actual scope must match, because an operator reading 'All promotions are switched off' will stop looking.
verifier_note: Directionally right, but four supporting claims are wrong and they were carrying the severity. (a) 'Loyalty tiers have no kill switch at all — not this one, not any' is FALSE: tier_fee_bps filters `where t.enabled`, and admin/app/(console)/pricing/actions.ts:77 toggles fee_tiers.enabled per row from the console. (b) 'bonus_ledger has no budget_cents of its own … it keeps going until the ledger is drained' is misleading: accrue_referral_bonus (20260806250000:88-99) charges the campaign with an increment-is-the-check UPDATE (`redemptions_used < max_redemptions and spent_cents + bonus_cents <= budget_cents`) and DELETES the ledger row when that UPDATE matches nothing, so every credit on the ledger is already funded and counted against budget_cents and continued accrual is bounded by the same budget. Exposure is bounded flag-on or flag-off, and spending a vested credit is delivery of an already-incurred, already-charged liability, not new loss. (c) 'The only remaining lever is hand-written SQL' is false: accrual requires an active kind='bonus' promotion (:64-69, `status='active' and starts_at <= now() and (ends_at is null or ends_at > now())`), so status='paused' and ends_at both stop it. (d) The console sentence is literally accurate — 'No code redeems and no grant applies to a new booking' is true of promo_codes and promo_grants, the gated paths; only the bold headline 'All promotions are switched off' overstates. What remains is a genuine scope-versus-claim mismatch that could mislead an operator mid-incident, with bounded economics and working alternative levers: low, not medium.

title: bonus_cash_payout_enabled has zero consumers — the flag credited with preventing cash farming is read by nothing
summary: The key is seeded false with a note describing what turning it on would enable. A repo-wide grep finds exactly two references: this INSERT and one comment in the referral migration. No SQL function, no edge function, and no console page reads it. The property everyone attributes to it — 'cash payout is off, so the classic farming target is closed' — is supplied entirely by the absence of any payout code, not by the flag.
trigger: Someone implements bonus cash payout (bonus_ledger.delivery='cash' exists as a column value already, and consume_fee_credit filters `delivery = 'credit'`, so the cash branch is a schema-level TODO). They ship the transfer path without a flag check, because the flag reads false and looks like it is already doing the gating. Meanwhile /flags shows bonus_cash_payout_enabled as 'paused' and the page's danger banner says users hitting it get a 'temporarily unavailable' message — an assurance with nothing behind it. The inverse failure is equally live today: an operator who flips it ON during an incident review changes nothing, and gets a success toast saying normal behaviour was restored.
money_impact: Today: zero direct loss, because no cash path exists. The exposure is the safety property being load-bearing in documentation and in this audit's own model ("app_flags.bonus_cash_payout_enabled is OFF; cash is the classic farming target") while being enforced by nothing. A cash bonus is the one delivery channel not bounded by the fee-headroom clamp — a credit can never exceed platform_fee_cents - stripe_floor, but cash leaves the platform balance at face value — so the first implementation that misses the check turns a bounded incentive into an unbounded one, and the switch that was supposed to be the backstop will read 'paused' the whole time.
evidence: supabase/migrations/20260806070000_promotions.sql:223-229 — the only INSERT: `('bonus_cash_payout_enabled', false, 'OFF. Bonuses accrue as fee CREDITS only. Turning this on enables real transfers off the platform balance…')`. `grep -rn "bonus_cash_payout_enabled" supabase admin src web` returns exactly two hits: that seed and a prose comment at supabase/migrations/20260806080000_referral_bonus.sql:23. consume_fee_credit (20260806080000:170) filters `state = 'payable' and delivery = 'credit'` — the cash branch simply has no consumer. admin/app/(console)/flags/page.tsx:46-52 renders every off flag under "Users hitting these get a 'temporarily unavailable' message."
fix_sketch: Add the check at the point of truth now, before the payout path exists: make vest_bonuses refuse to move a `delivery='cash'` row to 'payable' unless app_flag('bonus_cash_payout_enabled'), and add a control that fires on any bonus_ledger row with delivery='cash' and state in ('payable','paid') while the flag is off. That way the flag is enforced by code that runs today, and the future implementer inherits a guard rather than a comment.
verifier_note: Severity medium is overstated, and the finding both overstates the console exposure and misses the one concrete present-day consequence. Overstated: admin/app/(console)/promotions/actions.ts:57-62 never sets bonus_delivery on insert, so every console-created campaign defaults to 'credit' — a cash campaign cannot be created from the console at all, only by hand in the SQL editor. And the inverse failure is fail-SAFE: flipping the flag ON also does nothing, so an operator cannot accidentally open a cash channel. Missed: if a cash campaign IS hand-created, accrue_referral_bonus mints delivery='cash' rows, vest_bonuses (20260806080000:143-152) moves them pending -> payable with no delivery filter and no flag check, and consume_fee_credit then ignores them forever — producing a permanently growing, unsettleable 'Bonus owed (payable)' figure on the /promotions tile (page.tsx, bonusBy('payable')) that no code path can discharge. That is the accurate live consequence and it is what makes the proposed vest_bonuses guard the right fix, for a different reason than the one given. With no cash path, no console route to create one and no money moving: low.

title: /flags renders config rows as boolean kill switches and documents only 5 of the 10 keys it can toggle
summary: The page lists every app_flags row with an on/paused pill and a toggle, and its "Where each flag is enforced" section names only signups/posting/payments/tips/assistant. The other five keys — promotions_enabled, bonus_cash_payout_enabled, safety_alert, controls_alert, stripe_mode — are toggleable with no documentation of what they do, and for stripe_mode the `enabled` column has no meaning at all (the control reads `value->>'mode'`, never `enabled`).
trigger: An admin on /flags sees stripe_mode listed with a toggle. Flipping it writes an audit row (flag.disable), returns "stripe_mode is OFF. Users hitting that feature now get a 'temporarily paused' message", and adds stripe_mode to the red "features are currently paused" banner. Nothing changes: no code reads app_flags.stripe_mode.enabled. Conversely, an admin flipping controls_alert or safety_alert off gets the same generic user-facing wording, which does not tell them they have just silenced safety paging or the entire control framework's outbound channel.
money_impact: No direct loss. It is the substrate for the first finding: the console gives the two alerting kill switches the same appearance and the same reassuring copy as a routine feature pause, so the act of permanently blinding the monitoring system is presented to the operator as "users see a temporarily unavailable message." Nothing on the page distinguishes a flag that degrades a user feature from a flag that degrades detection.
evidence: admin/app/(console)/flags/page.tsx:46-52 — the banner applies uniformly to `(flags ?? []).filter((f) => !f.enabled)`; :61-77 renders a FlagToggle for every row; :82-89 — the enforcement list has exactly five <li>. admin/app/(console)/flags/actions.ts:55-57 — the success message is unconditional: "Users hitting that feature now get a 'temporarily paused' message." supabase/migrations/20260806350000_controls_always_on.sql:182 reads `value->>'mode'` for stripe_mode and never consults `enabled`.
fix_sketch: Add a `kind` column (or derive from key) so app_flags rows separate 'feature switch' from 'dispatch config' from 'declared mode'. Render config rows without a boolean toggle (or with an explicit "this silences alerting" confirmation and a required expiry), keep the user-facing copy only for feature switches, and generate the enforcement list from the same table so a new key cannot be added without a documented enforcement point.
verifier_note: The headline count and the entire stripe_mode scenario are wrong, and a stronger point was missed. Wrong: no migration seeds a 'stripe_mode' row (repo-wide grep returns only the 20260806350000:173 comment and :182 read) and setFlag refuses unknown keys (actions.ts:47-50, 'Flags are seeded by migration, not created here'), so the row does not exist, is not listed on /flags and cannot be toggled — the described trigger cannot happen, and the claim that its `enabled` column has no meaning is moot because the column has no row. The page lists NINE seeded keys, not ten: signups_enabled, payments_enabled, posting_enabled, tips_enabled, assistant_enabled (documented) plus safety_alert, controls_alert, promotions_enabled, bonus_cash_payout_enabled (undocumented). Missed and more valuable: bonus_cash_payout_enabled is seeded `enabled = false` (20260806070000:224), so in the steady state /flags ALWAYS renders the red '1 feature is currently paused' banner claiming users get a 'temporarily unavailable' message for a flag no code reads. A danger banner that is permanently lit is a danger banner nobody reads — which is exactly how flipping controls_alert off would be absorbed into the existing red without registering. Severity low is correct.

title: The admin login throttle has zero callers — no lockout exists, and ctl_admin_login_bruteforce is permanently blind
summary: 20260806090000_admin_roles.sql ships admin_login_attempts, admin_login_blocked() and record_admin_login() as the documented "5 failures per account / 15 min, 20 per IP" throttle. Nothing in the repository calls either function. The console's login page authenticates straight from the browser with supabase.auth.signInWithPassword, so no attempt — success or failure — is ever recorded and no block is ever consulted. The table is therefore always empty, which means ctl_admin_login_bruteforce (which SELECTs only from that table) returns zero rows on every sweep and reports the console as healthy forever.
trigger: Attacker obtains an admin email (e.g. from a support ticket or the public app) and POSTs password guesses at the Supabase GoTrue /token endpoint or the console login form. No per-account or per-IP lockout fires because record_admin_login is never called; the only remaining barrier is TOTP. Meanwhile the hourly sweep runs ctl_admin_login_bruteforce, gets 0 rows, records last_violations = 0, last_error = null, and the daily digest reports the security domain clean.
money_impact: The admin console holds the SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and is the only path to Stripe refunds and hold releases (admin-payment-action). A single-factor compromise is the first half of a chain that ends in arbitrary refunds against the platform balance. The second-order loss is worse: this is exactly the control that migration 20260806280000_watch_disabled_controls.sql was written about ("ctl_admin_login_bruteforce ... was disabled at 02:26 on 2026-08-12 ... Every sweep afterwards reported '0 errored, 0 stale'"). The remediation re-enabled a control that has never had a data source, so the system now reports confidently on a signal that cannot exist. A blind control that reports success is worse than no control, because it manufactures confidence.
evidence:
admin/app/login/page.tsx:20 — `const { error: err } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });` (client component; no server action, no throttle call).

Repo-wide grep for the three throttle identifiers returns ONLY the migration that defines them:
  $ grep -rn "admin_login_blocked|record_admin_login|admin_login_attempts" admin/app admin/lib supabase web src scripts
  supabase/migrations/20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:48,56,57,58,59,61,62,63,68,76,80,85,91,94,95,96,97,112
  (no hits in admin/, supabase/functions/, web/, or src/)

supabase/migrations/20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:100-117 — `create or replace function public.ctl_admin_login_bruteforce() ... from public.admin_login_attempts where not ok and created_at > now() - interval '1 hour' group by lower(email) having count(*) >= 10`

admin/app/login/page.tsx has one commit in its history (`8f17c3d Add internal admin console (v1)`), predating the 2026-08-06 throttle migration — it was never wired up.
fix_sketch: Move sign-in behind a server action: call admin_login_blocked(email, ip) before attempting the password, attempt signInWithPassword server-side, then call record_admin_login(email, ip, ok) on both branches. Until then, ctl_admin_login_bruteforce should be marked external or removed rather than left reporting green on an empty table.
verifier_note: Two corrections to the severity story. (1) The chain to money is longer than stated: requireAdmin re-checks the aal2 claim on EVERY request (guard.ts) and admin_users.status must be 'active', so a brute-forced password alone does not reach the service-role console — the attacker must also defeat TOTP, and /mfa's auto-enrolment only helps an account with NO verified factor, which ctl_admin_without_mfa separately watches. The proven loss is therefore the dead control plus the missing first-factor lockout, not a refund path. (2) The data the control wants does partly exist and the finding misses it: GoTrue's auth.audit_log_entries is already read by public.admin_user_login_history (20260705040000:78-95), so the fix does not require a server action at all — the control could be re-pointed at the auth audit log. Downgraded critical → high.

title: Pricing, promotions, controls and moderation write the admin_audit_log row AFTER the mutation, so a committed change is reported to the operator as a failure and leaves no record
summary: The console's documented and near-universal ordering is audit-then-mutate, fail-closed (see admin/lib/audit.ts and the comment at users/[id]/actions.ts:53-58 describing this exact bug being fixed). Five surfaces still do the opposite. setPlatformRate inserts the new platform_rates row at :47 and only audits at :55; the audit throw is swallowed by the catch at :66 which returns "Could not set the rate." The same inversion exists in grantToUsers (:122 rpc, :127 audit), setTier, saveTier, deleteTier, all six promotions actions, setControlEnabled, resolveFinding, resolveReport and reopenReport. cancelScheduledRate in the SAME FILE (:259) gets it right and its comment states the rule the rest of the file breaks.
trigger: Admin sets the platform take rate to 15% with a written justification. The platform_rates INSERT succeeds. The subsequent admin_audit_log INSERT fails (transient DB error, connection reset, PostgREST timeout — audit() throws on any error by design). The action returns { ok: false, message: "Could not set the rate." }. The rate is now live for every booking made from that instant, there is no audit row naming who changed it or why, and the operator believes nothing happened. If they retry with a blank effective date, a SECOND platform_rates row lands a few seconds later; if they retry with the same explicit date, platform_rates_effective_uniq rejects it with a raw constraint error that reads like the first attempt also failed.
money_impact: The take rate is the highest-leverage number in the product and comes out of the earner's payout. An unrecorded, unacknowledged rate change silently moves margin on every subsequent booking with no attribution. The same shape applies to grantToUsers, which can issue up to 500 promo grants and then report "Could not issue those grants" with 500 live grants outstanding and no audit row; to promotion.create/status/mint_codes/edit/clone/revoke_grant, which commit budget and revoke a named person's benefit unrecorded; and to control.disable, which additionally breaks ctl_control_disabled's own attribution — that control reads admin_audit_log for action='control.disable' to report `disabled_by`, so a control switched off without its audit row shows disabled_by: null, i.e. detection turned off by nobody.
fix_sketch: Wrap these actions in the same run() helper bookings/actions.ts and users/[id]/actions.ts already use: requireFresh → audit(intent) → mutate → auditRead(outcome). At minimum move the audit() call above the write in setPlatformRate, grantToUsers and setControlEnabled.
verifier_note: Three overstatements. (1) "The console's documented and near-universal ordering is audit-then-mutate" is half false — admin/lib/audit.ts's own header instructs the opposite: "call audit() after the action succeeds and let a failure surface as an error." The console carries two contradictory documented conventions; audit-first is documented only in the two run() helpers and one comment. (2) The retry scenarios are weaker than claimed: grant_promotion_to_users (20260806120000:196-200) inserts ON CONFLICT (user_id, promotion_id) DO NOTHING behind promo_grants_one_per_user_promo, so a retry cannot double-grant, and a repeated setPlatformRate at the same fee_bps is a no-op for fee_bps_at() (latest row ≤ now, identical value). What survives is the real defect: a committed change with no audit row, reported to the operator as a failure. (3) It requires a transient audit-insert failure while the same service client's prior write succeeded — a latent fail-open, not an everyday event. Downgraded high → medium.

title: /promotions — the console's only budget-spending surface — has no MFA step-up, while every comparable surface does
summary: All seven mutating promotions actions use requireAdmin("admin"), not requireFreshAdmin. Pricing, flags, team, user actions and booking money interventions all use requireFreshAdmin("admin"|"finance") with a 300s window and a ReauthPrompt retry path; PromoControls.tsx is the only money surface with no useStepUp/ReauthPrompt import at all. The same capability reached from /pricing (grantToUsers, pricing/actions.ts:106) DOES require step-up, so the identical grant is gated or ungated depending on which page you route through. createPromotion validates budget_dollars only as `> 0` — there is no ceiling.
trigger: Attacker holds a hijacked-but-valid admin session (stolen laptop, exfiltrated cookie, borrowed unlocked screen) whose TOTP was satisfied hours ago — precisely the threat guard.ts:64-78 names as the reason step-up exists ("AAL2 proves MFA happened at SOME point in this session. It does not prove the person at the keyboard right now is the one who passed it"). They cannot change the platform rate, flip a flag, touch the team, or refund a booking — all of those return stale_mfa. They CAN: createPromotion(kind='fee_override', fee_pct=0, budget_dollars=1000000, max_redemptions=999999) → setPromotionStatus('active') → mintCodes(count=200, seats=1000) → publish the codes. They can also editPromotion to raise budget_cents and extend ends_at on an already-live campaign, and revokeGrant to strip a named user's benefit.
money_impact: Loss is bounded by promotions.budget_cents and max_redemptions — but on this path the ATTACKER chooses both, and createPromotion imposes no upper bound on either (promotions/actions.ts:36-38 checks only `budgetDollars > 0`; maxRedemptions is `Math.max(1, Math.round(...))` with no cap). 200 codes × 1000 seats = 200,000 redemption seats against a self-declared budget. Each fee_override redemption forgoes the full platform fee on that booking down to the Stripe processing floor, so the realised loss is (budget or 200k × per-booking fee headroom, whichever binds first) — a ceiling set by the person who should not have authority at all. revokeGrant additionally lets them take away benefits users legitimately hold, one named person at a time, with no step-up.
fix_sketch: Switch all seven to requireFreshAdmin("admin"), wire useStepUp + ReauthPrompt into PromoControls.tsx (the helper exists precisely so "the next surface gets it by construction"), and impose an absolute budget ceiling in createPromotion/editPromotion the way setPlatformRate clamps the rate to 5–30%.
verifier_note: Two mechanical corrections. (1) "every comparable surface does" is false — controls/actions.ts setControlEnabled (turning DETECTION off), jobs/actions.ts, categories/actions.ts, access/actions.ts, disputes/actions.ts and moderation/actions.ts all use plain requireAdmin too. The accurate claim is that step-up covers exactly five surfaces and promotions is the largest money lever outside them. (2) The economics are wrong by orders of magnitude. Seats are not losses. consume_promo_grant (final definition, 20260806220000:269) charges least(max_benefit_cents, promo_benefit_cents(amount, fee_bps)), and promo_benefit_cents (:72-81) is the difference of two platform_fee_cents results — which floors at Stripe cost, ceil(amt*0.029)+30+25. On a $50 booking at the standing 10%: fee 500c, floor 200c, so the maximum forgone is 300c, and only when a REAL booking happens. 200,000 seats do not cost $1M; realised loss ≈ 6.8% of GMV transacted by grant holders during the window. Also, createPromotion lands as status='draft' and requires a separate activation, and codes must reach real users before any grant exists. Downgraded high → medium.

title: The 'finance' tier cannot move money — three layers disagree and the effective authority is 'admin' only
summary: admin-payment-action is the console's only path to Stripe. Its gate (adminAuth.ts:158-160) requires role === 'admin' exactly; adminAuth's AdminRole type does not even contain 'finance' or 'trust'. The console's bookings run() helper grants the same actions to requireFreshAdmin("finance"). And InterventionPanel is handed isAdmin = (ctx.role === "admin") and renders "Intervening on a booking requires the admin role" for anyone else. So the finance tier is granted the capability at exactly one of three layers and can exercise none of it.
trigger: A finance-tier operator opens /bookings/<id> to issue a refund. The panel refuses to render any control (isAdmin false). If they craft the POST directly, the console-side requireFreshAdmin("finance") passes, forceComplete/reopen/clearStartedAt write through the service role, but refundPayment/releaseHold/recordReversal reach admin-payment-action and come back 403 forbidden; the console surfaces the bare string "forbidden" via `String(body.message ?? body.error)`.
money_impact: Fails closed, so no unauthorised movement — but it recreates the exact failure the four-tier split was written to eliminate. 20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:11-15 states the reason for splitting tiers was that "one person's availability was a money-harm control." Today every refund, hold release and chargeback reversal still requires the single full-admin account; a finance hire can read /payments and do nothing. The predictable operational response is to grant 'admin' to whoever needs to refund, which collapses the tier model and hands them team management, flags, pricing and promotions as well. Separately, a finance-tier operator CAN write bookings.status/earner_done/poster_done directly through forceComplete (bookings/actions.ts:113-117) — the one money-adjacent write that does work for them is the one that bypasses the mutual-completion consent rule.
fix_sketch: Pick one layer as the truth. Either widen adminAuth to the four ranked tiers and let requireAdminCaller(req, 'finance', 300) admit finance and admin (then pass roleSatisfies-equivalent logic into InterventionPanel instead of ctx.role === 'admin'), or narrow bookings/actions.ts run() to requireFreshAdmin("admin") and delete the finance tier's claim to refunds from guard.ts and the migration comment.
verifier_note: Severity is overstated for two reasons the finding does not weigh.
