(1) There is no finance operator: 20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:29-31 states the production table holds exactly the one original admin row and this migration adds no others, so today this is a latent design inconsistency with zero operational impact — the "finance hire can do nothing" harm is prospective. (2) forceCancel actually fails closed correctly for finance too: it calls release_hold through admin-payment-action BEFORE writing status (bookings/actions.ts:213-219) and throws "Booking NOT cancelled" on the 403, so no half-state. The residual real point is narrow and correct: forceComplete / reopenBooking / clearStartedAt are direct service-role writes a finance-tier operator can make without admin. That is a tier question, not a broken guard — guard_bookings_write's service_role early-return is deliberate and every call is audited intent-first. Downgraded medium → low.

title: admin-payment-action can reach Stripe with no admin_audit_log row, and its own header asserts the opposite
summary: The function's header claims "The console writes its admin_audit_log row BEFORE calling this, so an action that reaches Stripe is always already on the record." Nothing enforces that. The function authenticates the admin's own user JWT (the same token sitting in the console operator's browser), performs no audit write of its own, and is reachable by a plain POST that never touches the Next.js console. A refund issued that way leaves no admin_audit_log entry at all.
trigger: Any active 'admin'-role operator (or anyone holding their session, with a TOTP satisfied in the last 300s) copies the access token out of the browser and POSTs {bookingId, op:'refund', reason:'x', amountCents:N} to /functions/v1/admin-payment-action. Both auth checks pass, Stripe issues the refund with reverse_transfer, record_refund updates the ledger — and admin_audit_log gains nothing.
money_impact: The append-only, UPDATE/DELETE-revoked admin_audit_log is the platform's entire accountability record for money movement (20260705010000:41). This path defeats it. The residual trail is payments.refunded_by / refund_reason, which are SINGLE columns overwritten by record_refund on every call (20260804020000:112-113) — so a sequence of partial refunds preserves only the last actor and last reason, and the amounts are collapsed into a running refunded_cents total. No control detects it: ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered is the only reversal control and it is explicitly blind to this shape, because admin-payment-action stamps refund_source='admin' before calling Stripe (index.ts:189) and stripe-webhook early-returns for that source, so no disputes row is filed and the ledger IS updated. There is no ctl_* that joins Stripe refunds or payments.refunded_at against admin_audit_log.
fix_sketch: Have admin-payment-action write its own admin_audit_log row (admin_id = caller, action = 'payment.<op>.edge', detail = booking/amount/reason/refund_id) immediately before the Stripe call, and de-duplicate against the console's row on the /audit page rather than relying on the console being the only caller. Alternatively require a console-minted nonce that the function verifies against a freshly written audit row.
verifier_note: One material omission that softens it: every refund carries metadata: { booking_id, admin_id, reason } on the Stripe refund object itself (index.ts:188), so per-refund attribution DOES survive per-call — outside the DB, in Stripe, where the finding says nothing survives but a collapsed refunded_by. The gap is that the platform's own append-only record is silent, and no control reconciles Stripe refunds against it. Also note the threat model: the actor must already hold an active 'admin' row plus a second factor satisfied within 300s, and the normal console path DOES audit intent-first (bookings/actions.ts:38-42) — so this is an insider-accountability hole and a scripting bypass, not privilege escalation. Severity medium is right.

title: addTeamMember can strand the console with no admin — it bypasses both the self-check and assertNotLastAdmin
summary: setTeamStatus and setTeamRole both guard against lockout (no acting on yourself; assertNotLastAdmin). addTeamMember has neither, and it upserts on user_id with status forced to 'pending'. Because requireAdmin refuses any row whose status is not 'active' (guard.ts:151), re-adding an existing active admin — including yourself — instantly revokes their access. Note also that the guards on the other two actions are vacuous: the actor is by construction an active admin and cannot target themselves, so admin_active_admin_count() is always ≥ 2 when assertNotLastAdmin runs. The one path that can actually produce the lockout is the one without the guard.
trigger: Sole admin (the current production state per 20260806090000: "The existing single admin keeps 'admin'. There are no other admin_users rows") types their own address into the Add-teammate form — e.g. to correct a role or a note. The upsert sets their own row to status 'pending'. Their next request fails requireAdmin at guard.ts:151 and redirects to /denied. Every subsequent console request does the same. Recovery requires Supabase database credentials, which 20260804030000_admin_team_lifecycle.sql:12-15 names as "exactly the wrong dependency."
money_impact: The console is the only path to refunds, hold releases, chargeback reversals, dispute resolution (which is what unblocks earner-claim-payment settlement), flags and the promotions kill switches. With no admin able to sign in, every one of those is frozen until someone with direct DB access restores the row — during which any earner blocked by an open dispute stays unpaid and any escrow hold nearing its ~7-day expiry cannot be released or captured from the console. It also disables the operator's ability to pause payments via /flags in an incident.
fix_sketch: In addTeamMember: refuse when userId === ctx.user.id, and call assertNotLastAdmin(ctx, userId) before the upsert (or make the upsert not downgrade an already-'active' row — e.g. only set status:'pending' on insert). Also fix setTeamRole to call assertNotLastAdmin for any role other than 'admin', not just 'support', since trust and finance cannot manage the team either.
verifier_note: One addition the finding half-states: setTeamRole's guard is wrong in a second way its own comment concedes. The check is `if (role === "support") await assertNotLastAdmin(...)` (:180), so demoting an admin to 'finance' or 'trust' skips it entirely — while the comment at :168-170 explicitly says demoting the last admin to finance would still strand the console, because trust and finance cannot manage the team. The comment describes a guard the code does not implement (and which would be vacuous anyway).

title: Support tier browses the full user table with email addresses, contradicting its own tier definition
summary: The four-tier split defines support as "tickets, and a user's own context. NOT bulk PII, NOT all payments" (guard.ts:16-17, and 20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:7-9 names support's read-everything reach as "least privilege inverted"). /users is gated at requireAdminPage("support") and renders an email column for every account, paginated and searchable.
trigger: A support-tier operator opens /users, pages through the directory or searches by any substring, and reads every account's email address alongside name and username. No booking, ticket or other relationship to the operator is required.
money_impact: No direct money loss, and it is audited (auditRead 'user.list' / 'user.search' at :56 and :67), so it is a documented-intent mismatch rather than a silent one. It matters here because the tier model is the thing this dimension relies on: the migration that introduced the tiers justified them by naming this exact exposure as the problem being fixed, and the fix did not reach the page. If the tier boundaries are trusted to be accurate elsewhere (they are cited as the reason support may safely read money pages), that trust is misplaced.
evidence: admin/app/(console)/users/page.tsx:40 — `const ctx = await requireAdminPage("support");` admin/app/(console)/users/page.tsx:155 — `{u.email ?? "—"}` admin/app/(console)/users/page.tsx:66-67 — `// Browsing exposes the same emails a search does — same audit weight.` / `await auditRead(ctx, "user.list", "search", ...)` supabase/migrations/20260806090000_admin_roles.sql:5-9 — "'support' could READ everything — every user's PII ... That is least privilege inverted" ... and the tier definition at :16 — "support tickets, and a user's own context. NOT bulk PII".
fix_sketch: Either raise the /users list route to "trust" (or gate the email column on roleSatisfies(ctx.role, "trust")) while leaving id-addressed /users/[id] at support for ticket context, or amend the tier definitions in guard.ts and the migration comment to say support does have directory-level PII.
verifier_note: Two qualifiers. It is latent, not live: per 20260806090000:29-31 there are no support-tier rows in admin_users today, so nobody currently holds this reach. And the finding's supporting sentence "they are cited as the reason support may safely read money pages" is inaccurate — /payments is gated at requireAdminPage("finance") (payments/page.tsx:15) and Nav.tsx:50 marks it minRole finance; only /bookings and /bookings/[id] sit at support. Low is the right severity: a documented-intent mismatch on an unpopulated tier, fully audited.

title: The tip rail is a 0%-cost value-transfer channel the platform SUBSIDISES, and its $200 per-booking cap is unlocked by a booking nobody ever pays for
summary: guard_tip_caps sizes the per-booking tip cap as greatest(captured_cents * 2, 20000), where captured_cents sums only payments at status='captured'. But guard_bookings_write lets a booking reach 'completed' on earner_done && poster_done with NO captured payment, and stripe-tip gates only on status in ('completed','verified'). So a colluding pair reaches the tip channel with captured=0, the cap falls to its $200 floor, and the escrow hold that made the booking 'confirmed' is simply never captured — it lapses on Stripe's ~7-day timer and the poster is charged nothing. The tip PaymentIntent carries transfer_data.destination with NO application_fee_amount (stripe-tip/index.ts:115-123), so the full amount transfers to the earner and Stripe's processing comes out of the PLATFORM balance. The remaining cap, $500/24h, is scoped to the POSTER only — there is no per-earner and no global limit — so N poster shells feed one KYC'd earner linearly.
trigger: Poster account P and earner account E (same person). P posts a $10 gig; E books it; P accepts (a $10 manual-capture hold is placed, accept-booking only requires pi.status==='requires_capture'). Both tap 'mark done' -> guard_bookings_write:135 advances status to 'completed'. P never taps Verify & Rate, so nothing is ever captured. tip_headroom_cents now returns 20000c because no captured payment exists. P sends 3 tips totalling $200. Repeat over 3 bookings/day to hit the $500/24h poster cap. The three $10 holds expire uncaptured on day 7 and P is never billed a cent.
money_impact: Attacker cost per poster shell per day: $0.00 (all holds lapse uncaptured; only $30 of card credit is temporarily tied up). Value moved: $500/day, 100% of it landing in E's Connect balance and paid out daily (stripe-connect-onboard/index.ts:196 sets payouts.schedule.interval='daily', no delay_days). Platform cost per shell-day, using the code's own Stripe model (ceil(amount*0.029)+30 per charge): $200 tip = 580+30 = 610c, x2 = 1220c; $100 tip = 290+30 = 320c; total 1540c = $15.40/day out of pocket, against $0.00 revenue. Compare the gig rail for the same $500: platform_fee_after_credit floors at ceil(50000*0.029)+30+25 = 1505c, so moving $500 through gigs costs the mover 3.01% and nets the platform +25c. The tip rail costs the mover 0.00% and nets the platform -$15.40 — a 3.01-point arbitrage in favour of the laundering path, on identical money. At 1,000 users with 20 poster shells: $308/day = $112,420/yr of direct subsidy, plus $10,000/day of chargeback-eligible value sitting in connected accounts that pay out in ~2 business days. This directly violates the invariant the rest of the pricing design is built on — platform_fee_cents floors at ceil(amount*0.029)+30+25 precisely 'so a 0% promotion can never settle at a loss', and consume_fee_credit refuses to spend past the floor because 'We never pay Stripe's processing to honour a credit'. Tips bypass both. NO CONTROL BOUNDS THIS: the full ctl_* registry contains no tip-volume, per-earner, or negative-margin control; ctl_earner_credit_missing only checks tips charged-but-not-credited. RUNBOOK_MONEY.md:139-142 asserts the caps close the laundering vector — they do not, because the cap floor is reachable at zero cost and the velocity cap has no earner-side counterpart. The tip_caps header names the 0% take rate and the chargeback exposure but names NEITHER the zero-cost unlock NOR that the platform pays processing out of pocket on every tip, including legitimate ones.
evidence:
supabase/migrations/20260804000000_tip_caps.sql:125 — `v_cap_cents := greatest(v_captured_cents * 2, 20000);` where v_captured_cents comes from `where p.status = 'captured'` (zero for an uncaptured booking).
supabase/migrations/20260730140000_pin_booking_insert_columns.sql:135 — `or (old.status = 'confirmed' and new.status = 'completed' and new.earner_done and new.poster_done)` — no captured-payment predicate (contrast the completed->verified branch immediately below, which DOES require `p.status = 'captured'`).
supabase/functions/stripe-tip/index.ts:52-55 — `if (!['completed', 'verified'].includes(booking.status))`.
supabase/functions/stripe-tip/index.ts:115-123 — `stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount, ..., transfer_data: { destination: earnerAcct.account_id } })` with no `application_fee_amount`.
supabase/migrations/20260804000000_tip_caps.sql:145 — `if v_poster_24h + new.amount_cents > 50000` — the only velocity cap, keyed on `j.poster_id`; no earner-side equivalent anywhere in the file.
fix_sketch: (1) Gate stripe-tip on an actually-captured payment for the booking, not on booking.status — a tip is a top-up on money that moved, so require payments.status='captured' and drop the $200 floor to a multiple of what was captured. (2) Charge an application_fee_amount on tips at least equal to platform_fee_cents(tip, 0) (the processing floor), so the platform never funds Stripe out of pocket. (3) Add a per-EARNER 24h tip-receipt cap in guard_tip_caps mirroring the poster one, and a ctl_tip_velocity_anomaly control on tips received per earner across distinct posters.
verifier_note: Drop the 'zero-cost unlock' framing entirely — the $200 cap floor is unconditional and reached identically by a normally captured small gig, so the uncaptured-booking path changes only ~$1 of avoided platform fee per booking. Restate as: (a) tips carry no application_fee_amount on a destination charge, so the platform pays 2.9%+30c out of pocket on EVERY tip including legitimate ones — a negative unit margin the tip_caps header does not name (it names only the 0% take rate and the chargeback exposure); (b) the $500/24h velocity cap is poster-scoped with no earner-side counterpart, so tip receipt per earner is unbounded across shells; (c) no ctl_* control observes tip volume, tips-per-earner, or distinct-poster fan-in. Maximum subsidy at the existing caps is $15.40/day per funded poster shell, and the attacker's 'value moved' is their own charged card, not platform funds.

title: The unpaid-worker control was silently gutted: a later redefinition dropped both `earner_done` and the 'confirmed' status, so the ghosted-poster case it exists for can no longer fire
summary: ctl_escrow_hold_expiring_work_done is defined twice. The original (20260806040000:174-179) filters `coalesce(b.earner_done, false) and b.status in ('confirmed','completed')`. The LIVE definition — 20260806150000, whose stated purpose is only to re-anchor the hold age onto payments.authorized_at — reproduces the function with a different WHERE: the `earner_done` predicate is gone entirely and the status set becomes ('completed','verified'). A ghosted booking never reaches either: advance_mutual_completion only promotes 'confirmed' -> 'completed' when earner_done AND poster_done are both true, and a ghosting poster by definition never sets poster_done. So the control now excludes exactly the shape it was written for. It also silently regressed entity_id from b.id to p.id and dropped earner_id/poster_id/job_title/slot_id from the finding detail — the fields the control registry's own `why` text tells the operator to act on.
trigger: Earner does the work and taps 'mark done' -> bookings.earner_done = true, status stays 'confirmed' (advance_mutual_completion, 20260624210000:43 requires both flags). The poster never responds. The hold ages past day 5. run_all_controls() executes the live ctl_escrow_hold_expiring_work_done, whose WHERE requires b.status in ('completed','verified') — the row is 'confirmed', so it is not returned. No finding is filed, no page is sent, and on day 7 Stripe voids the authorization. Nobody is ever told there was a 48-hour window.
money_impact: The control's registered `why` prices the miss itself: 'there is a 24-48 hour window in which stripe-capture-payment or earner-claim-payment can still capture real money, after which there is nothing left to capture and no code change can conjure it back... Cost of a miss: a student worked for free.' Loss per miss is the full gig value to the earner — up to $10,000 (MAX_JOB_PAY, guard enforced at 20260730120000:49) — plus the platform's own fee on that booking (10% = up to $1,000), since an uncaptured hold means nobody is charged at all. The 'completed'/'verified' rows the control still returns are the benign cases: 'completed' means the poster already marked done and is engaged, and a 'verified' booking with an uncaptured hold is blocked outright by guard_bookings_write's completed->verified branch, which requires a captured payment. So in practice the control now fires almost exclusively on the case that does not need it, and never on the case that does. Per the control framework's own doctrine ('A control that errors or goes stale is reported as loudly as a violation — both mean you are no longer being told the truth'), this is a control reporting success while blind.
evidence:
ORIGINAL, supabase/migrations/20260806040000_control_library.sql:174-179:
```
where p.status = 'authorized'
  and coalesce(b.earner_done, false)
  and b.status in ('confirmed', 'completed')
  and h.at is not null
  and h.at < now() - interval '5 days'
```
LIVE (last definition in timestamp order), supabase/migrations/20260806150000_authorized_at.sql:83-88:
```
where p.status = 'authorized'
  and b.status in ('completed', 'verified')
  and coalesce(p.authorized_at, greatest(p.created_at, p.cancelled_at)) < now() - interval '5 days'
  and coalesce(p.authorized_at, greatest(p.created_at, p.cancelled_at)) >= now() - interval '8 days'
```
supabase/migrations/20260624210000_review4_db_fixes.sql:43 — `if new.earner_done and new.poster_done and new.status = 'confirmed' then new.status := 'completed';`
The 20260806150000 header claims the only change is the age anchor: 'the controls switch to coalesce(authorized_at, ...) so they keep working'. It says nothing about narrowing the population.
fix_sketch: Restore the original predicates in a new migration: `and coalesce(b.earner_done, false) and b.status in ('confirmed','completed')`, keeping the authorized_at anchor. Restore entity_id to b.id (booking) so existing open findings resolve, and restore earner_id/poster_id/job_title/slot_id to the detail. Add a drift test that asserts each ctl_ function's WHERE clause against a golden fixture, since a `create or replace` reproduction is the exact mechanism that lost it.
verifier_note: Accurate mechanism: 20260806150000 replaced the body wholesale and lost `coalesce(b.earner_done,false)` plus the 'confirmed' status, while also swapping entity_id from b.id to p.id and dropping earner_id/poster_id/job_title/slot_id from the detail. The lost population is specifically earner_done && status='confirmed'. The retained 'completed' rows are NOT benign — poster-marked-done-but-never-verified is a genuine at-risk shape and is what admin forceComplete creates — so the control is degraded, not inverted; only the 'verified' branch is near-empty (completed->verified requires a captured payment). Note additionally that the entity_id change means open findings keyed on booking ids and new ones keyed on payment ids are different rows, so the pre-change history for a still-violating booking auto-resolves rather than persisting as one row.

title: A worker on a 'Flexible' gig whose poster ghosts has NO settlement path at all — the client hides the claim button, the edge function refuses, and the console it points them to has no capture operation
summary: PostJobScreen creates the fallback slot as `{ id: 's1', label: 'Flexible — Contact to Schedule', taken: false }` with no startsAt, so job_slots.starts_at is NULL and guard_bookings_write derives bookings.starts_at as NULL. Three doors then close in sequence. (1) shared/lifecycle.js:59 returns false when startsAt is null, so EarnScreen never renders the 'Claim your payment' CTA — the earner is not merely blocked, they are never shown that a claim exists or that a hold is expiring. (2) earner-claim-payment returns NO_SCHEDULE with the message 'contact support to settle it'. (3) admin-payment-action, the console's ONLY money path, accepts exactly three ops — release_hold, refund, record_reversal. There is no capture op. Support cannot settle the booking. RUNBOOK_MONEY.md:105 additionally forbids the one remaining manual route: 'Do not capture from the Stripe Dashboard as a shortcut' (it fires payment_intent.succeeded, which credits the pre-computed full split without reading amount_received). The runbook's own 'It still cannot' list (§7) does not mention this gap.
trigger: Poster posts a gig without picking times (PostJobScreen actively encourages it: 'No times picked — your gig will show "Flexible — Contact to Schedule"'). Earner books the flexible slot, poster accepts, a hold is placed. Earner performs the work and marks done. Poster ghosts. Day 3: no CTA appears in EarnScreen because canClaimEarnerPayment sees startsAt === null. Day 7: Stripe voids the authorization. The earner opens a support ticket; the agent opens /bookings/<id>, and the Intervene menu offers only Release hold / Refund / Record chargeback. There is nothing to press.
money_impact: Full gig value lost to the worker, up to $10,000 per booking (MAX_JOB_PAY). The poster pays $0 — the hold lapses uncaptured — so the platform also loses its fee (up to $1,000 at the 1000 bps standing rate) and the transaction leaves no GMV. Recovery is an out-of-band apology payment from the operator's own funds, which no code path records. Exposure scales with adoption of flexible scheduling, which is a first-class, promoted product feature, not an edge case. NOTE ON THE EXISTING RESIDUAL: ctl_live_booking_without_schedule_anchor does name this slot and says 'WILL RETURN ROWS TODAY, and that is the point'. Two consequences it does NOT name. First, it is severity 'high' and its predicate (`b.status in ('confirmed','completed') and s.starts_at is null`) matches EVERY in-flight flexible booking, healthy or not — one open finding per ordinary booking, volume proportional to usage rather than to harm, which under controls_sweep_and_page's 'page only if something newly needs a human' rule pages on every routine flexible booking and trains operators to ignore the channel. Second, and decisively, the finding it raises has no remediation behind it: there is no capture op in admin-payment-action, so the control reports money it is impossible to move. A control that names a loss nobody has a tool to stop is a log line, not a control. And the second control that should have caught the same worker — ctl_escrow_hold_expiring_work_done — cannot fire at all on a ghosted 'confirmed' booking (see the separate finding).
evidence:
src/screens/PostJobScreen.js:201 — `: [{ id: 's1', label: 'Flexible — Contact to Schedule', taken: false }];` (no startsAt).
src/context/JobsContext.js:1119 — `job_slots.insert(... starts_at: s.startsAt || null)` -> NULL.
supabase/migrations/20260730140000_pin_booking_insert_columns.sql:94-99 — `if new.slot_id is not null then select s.starts_at into new.starts_at ... else new.starts_at := null;`
shared/lifecycle.js:59 — `if (!sched || isNaN(sched.getTime())) return false;  // need a scheduled time to anchor grace` — gates renderClaimCta in src/screens/EarnScreen.js:429.
supabase/functions/earner-claim-payment/index.ts — `return json({ error: 'NO_SCHEDULE', message: 'This booking has no scheduled time — contact support to settle it.' }, 409);`
supabase/functions/admin-payment-action/index.ts:49 — `if (op !== 'release_hold' && op !== 'refund' && op !== 'record_reversal') return json({ error: 'bad_op' }, 400);`
RUNBOOK_MONEY.md:105 — 'Do not capture from the Stripe Dashboard as a shortcut.'
fix_sketch: Add an admin `capture` op to admin-payment-action (admin tier + 300s step-up, reason required) that calls stripe-capture-payment's logic server-side, so the message 'contact support to settle it' becomes true. Independently, give the flexible slot a concrete starts_at at BOOKING time — when the earner books a flexible slot, require the pair to agree a datetime and write it to job_slots.starts_at — which restores the self-service claim path and drains ctl_live_booking_without_schedule_anchor's false-positive volume at the same time.
verifier_note: The three doors are real, but door one and two are documented, tested residuals — the finding's value is narrower and should be stated as such: the fallback both of them route to does not exist. Add an admin capture op (admin tier + 300s step-up + written reason, reconciled against amount_received like stripe-capture-payment) or correct RUNBOOK_MONEY §1.4 and the NO_SCHEDULE copy, which currently promise a settlement the console cannot perform. Severity is bounded by flexible-slot volume and by the poster still being able to verify pre-lapse, not by MAX_JOB_PAY.

title: Stolen-card cash-out: destination charges with no transfer reversal on chargeback, daily payouts, and zero velocity limits anywhere on the gig rail
summary: Every gig charge is a destination charge (transfer_data.destination, no on_behalf_of), so the platform is the merchant of record and bears disputes. The charge.dispute.created handler does exactly two things: file a disputes row and email an operator. It never reverses the transfer. The only reverse_transfer in the codebase is admin-payment-action's `op='refund'` — and that path is unusable on a disputed charge, as the code itself states in record_reversal: 'Stripe rejects refunds.create on a disputed charge (charge_disputed)'. record_reversal is therefore ledger-only: it adjusts payments.refunded_cents and debits the earner's DASHBOARD number, while the actual cash stays in the connected account and has already been paid out. Meanwhile the gig rail has no velocity limits of any kind — no per-poster daily spend cap, no per-account booking-rate cap, no new-card cooling period. The contrast is stark: the tip rail carries three caps (per booking, per count, per poster/24h) specifically because it was recognised as a laundering vector; the gig rail, which moves up to $10,000 per booking, carries none.
trigger: Attacker registers poster account P, saves a stolen card via stripe-create-setup-intent, and registers earner account E with a real or synthetic identity that clears Stripe Connect Express KYC. P posts a $10,000 gig; E books; P accepts (hold); both mark done; P verifies -> stripe-capture-payment captures and Stripe transfers to E's connected account. E's account has payouts.schedule.interval='daily' with no delay_days, so the cash reaches E's bank in ~2 business days. The cardholder disputes 5-60+ days later. The webhook files a disputes row and sends an email. Nothing pulls the money back.
money_impact: Arithmetic on one $10,000 gig at the 1000 bps standing rate. Charge 1,000,000c. platform_fee_cents(1000000,1000) = max(100000, ceil(29000)+30+25) = 100,000c application fee. Transfer to earner = 900,000c. Platform balance after capture: +1,000,000 - 29,030 (Stripe's 2.9%+30c, the code's own model) - 900,000 = +70,970c. Chargeback lost: -1,000,000 - 1,500 (dispute fee) => platform net -930,530c = -$9,305.30 per stolen $10,000, while the attacker's bank receives $9,000.00 (90.0% recovery on a stolen card). With a 0-bps loyalty tier or promo the fee floors at 29,055c, the earner receives $9,709.45 (97.1% recovery) and the platform's net loss rises to $10,014.75. Nothing in the code bounds repetition: MAX_JOB_PAY caps a single gig at $10,000 but there is no cap on gigs per day, per poster, or per card. A single card run to a $20,000 limit yields the attacker ~$18,000 and costs the platform ~$18,600 including dispute fees. WHAT ACTUALLY LIMITS IT TODAY: only Stripe Radar (not configured in this repo) and Connect Express KYC on the EARNER side — real friction, but one-time per farm rather than per-dollar, and reusable across unlimited stolen cards. WHAT DOES NOT: ID verification is optional for posters and only drives a badge (profiles.verified / id_verification_status); the disputes gate only blocks FUTURE auto-settlement on the same booking; there is no ctl_* control on chargeback rate, on new-account spend velocity, or on an earner receiving from many first-time posters. ctl_external_reversal_not_ledgered detects the accounting hole after the fact and only prompts a human to record it. The tip rail (see the separate finding) makes this worse, not better: it lets the same attacker skip capture entirely and cash out at 100% instead of 90%.
evidence:
supabase/functions/stripe-create-payment-intent/index.ts — `transfer_data: { destination: earnerAcct.account_id }` (no `on_behalf_of`, so the platform is liable for disputes).
supabase/functions/stripe-webhook/index.ts:281-307 — `case 'charge.dispute.created':` -> `recordReversal(...)` (inserts a disputes row) + an email. No `stripe.transfers.createReversal`, no `stripe.refunds.create`.
supabase/functions/admin-payment-action/index.ts:121-124 — record_reversal's own comment: 'A LOST CHARGEBACK takes the money back but is not a refund: Stripe rejects refunds.create on a disputed charge (charge_disputed)... This is the ledger-only path: no Stripe call'.
supabase/functions/admin-payment-action/index.ts:186-187 — `reverse_transfer: true, refund_application_fee: true` — reachable only under `op === 'refund'`, which requires `pay.status === 'captured'` and a charge Stripe will still let you refund.
supabase/functions/stripe-connect-onboard/index.ts:196 — `payouts: { schedule: { interval: 'daily' } }` with no `delay_days`.
`grep -rn 'reverse_transfer' supabase/` returns exactly one code hit, at admin-payment-action:186.
fix_sketch: (1) Add a `delay_days` to the Express payout schedule (7-14 days) so the payout window is longer than the capture-to-first-chargeback window for the common fraud patterns; the earner-claim path already tolerates multi-day settlement. (2) In the charge.dispute.created handler, call stripe.transfers.createReversal on the linked transfer up to the disputed amount before paging, so the loss lands on the party that received the funds rather than the platform balance. (3) Add per-poster gig-rail velocity caps mirroring guard_tip_caps (cents/24h and count/24h, tightened for accounts under N days old or on a first-seen card), enforced in stripe-create-payment-intent before the hold. (4) Add ctl_chargeback_rate_by_earner and ctl_new_account_spend_velocity so the exposure is at least observed.
verifier_note: Keep the asymmetry and the missing tooling, drop the framing as a novel exploit: the chargeback-eats-the-platform outcome is already stated in RUNBOOK_MONEY §2.4 and in the stripe-webhook H12 comment. The two additions that stand are (a) the webhook comment says a human can 'freeze/recover' but no code path can reverse a transfer post-dispute (refund errors with charge_disputed by admin-payment-action's own comment; record_reversal is ledger-only), and (b) there is no per-poster/per-card gig-rail velocity cap and no chargeback-rate or new-account-spend control, while the far smaller tip rail carries three caps. Note that a post-payout transfer reversal recovers little — prioritise delay_days on the Express payout schedule and velocity limits at hold time over the reversal call. The cited cents arithmetic is correct as written.
